image_description: A close-up, high-angle shot of a sea lion resting on a rocky surface. The animal's head is tucked down against its body/flipper, obscuring the face and eyes. The fur appears thick and coarse, transitioning from light tan to darker brown. A small external ear flap is visible on the side of the head. The background consists of out-of-focus grey rocks.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is angled downwards and tucked into the body, making the top of the skull and sagittal crest impossible to verify from this perspective.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: A distinct, small external ear flap is clearly visible on the side of the head, confirming it is an eared seal (sea lion) rather than a true seal.
The snout area is pressed against the body/rock and is largely out of frame or obscured by shadow/fur, making whisker verification impossible.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible fur texture is consistent with coarse marine mammal hair. The coloration is light tan/brown, which matches the 'lighter' description often seen in females or juveniles, though ventral comparison is limited by pose.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible curve of the back and neck suggests a large, robust, fusiform body typical of pinnipeds.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The neck area is obscured by the head position and angle; no mane is visible, but this may be due to gender (female/juvenile) or occlusion.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreflippers are not clearly isolated or visible in their entirety; the animal is curled up, hiding the limbs.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Hind flippers are completely out of frame or occluded by the body.
The asymmetrical pose (head tucked, body curved) prevents a direct visual assessment of bilateral symmetry.

artifact_observations.reasoning: The texture of the surface the sea lion is resting on (or its own tucked flipper) appears slightly smudged and lacks the distinct follicle definition seen in the upper neck fur, suggesting minor generative blur or fusion.
The nose tip blends somewhat indistinctly into the surrounding fur and shadow, lacking a sharp, defined boundary typical of a wet nose, though this could be due to image resolution.
